events.title: Kotlin 1.0 released
events.summary: JetBrains released [Kotlin] 1.0 on February 15, 2016 — the first stable version of the pragmatic [JVM] and [Android] language.
events.about: [Kotlin] 1.0 committed to backward compatibility for the language and standard library — safe for production [Android] and server code. Google later made [Kotlin] the preferred [Android] language. Null-safe types, data classes, and coroutines reduced boilerplate versus [Java].

narrative.whyChosen: [Kotlin] 1.0 was the stability milestone that let enterprises bet on [Kotlin] beyond experiments.
narrative.whyImportant: It unlocked Google's [Android] pivot and proved JetBrains could ship a mainstream [JVM] language.
narrative.problemSolved: Preview [Kotlin] changed frequently; teams needed a stable 1.0 with long-term compatibility guarantees.

events.title: Zig programming language announced
events.summary: On February 8, 2016, Andrew Kelley introduced [Zig] — a systems language aiming to be a simpler, safer alternative to C.
events.about: [Zig] targets low-level work — games, operating systems, compilers — with explicit memory control, compile-time code execution, and no hidden runtime surprises. It ships with a built-in build system and cross-compilation. Developers reach for it when C's bugs and C++'s complexity are too costly, but [Rust]'s strict rules feel too restrictive.

narrative.whyChosen: [Zig] reframed systems programming around explicit memory, simple builds, and easy C library integration.
narrative.whyImportant: It renewed interest in small systems languages and influenced how newer toolchains handle builds and cross-compilation.
narrative.problemSolved: Kelley hit friction integrating C libraries in [Go], memory bugs in C++, and [Rust]'s learning curve while building audio software.

events.title: Apple ordered to help FBI unlock San Bernardino iPhone
events.summary: A federal magistrate ordered Apple on February 16, 2016 to assist the FBI in bypassing security on an [iPhone] used by a San Bernardino shooter — sparking a national debate over encryption backdoors.
events.about: Apple refused to build a custom [iOS] version that would weaken passcode protections for all users. Tim Cook framed it as a civil-liberties line in the sand; the FBI eventually unlocked the phone with a third-party exploit. The fight shaped how platforms market device encryption, law-enforcement access requests, and the 'going dark' debate that still influences E2E messaging design.

narrative.whyChosen: The Apple–FBI fight defined the encryption [backdoor] debate for a generation of security engineers.
narrative.whyImportant: It cemented on-device encryption as a product differentiator platforms would not casually compromise.
narrative.problemSolved: Law enforcement wanted access to locked devices; Apple argued a master key would endanger every user.
